1.pericope_label: Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth; I have put my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles. He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street
debates: What the verb rendered uphold means: Clarke translates it on whom I lean, of a king leaning on his most trusted servant, while Calvin sets out both a passive sense, that God lays the whole charge on him, and an active one, that God raises him up, and objects to neither.
What the second verb of the second verse governs: Gill reports that it may mean not lifting up the voice but lifting up faces, that is, accepting persons, which is how one old version takes it.
outliers: Clarke argues that since all agree the first seven verses belong to Christ, and they continue the prophecy of the preceding chapter, that prophecy cannot belong to Cyrus.
Calvin explains the abrupt turn to Christ by the prophets’ habit of bringing him in whenever they promise something hard to believe, since in him all promises are ratified.
Clarke sets out the wide range of the word for judgment, from rule and plan to every stage of a legal process, and settles here on the law to be published by the Messiah.
Ellicott distinguishes the street, the open space where men harangued the people, from the gate, kept for the formal administration of justice.

3.pericope_label: A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth. He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law
debates: Whom the two figures stand for: Keil and Delitzsch report an early Latin father who made the bruised reed the faith of Israel and the glimmering wick the zeal of the Gentiles, and answer that the words hardly admit the distinction.

What the second verb of the fourth verse means: Keil and Delitzsch reject a derivation giving, he will not be rash or impetuous but execute his calling with wise moderation, since both verbs must echo the figures of the previous verse.
outliers: Calvin refuses to let the mildness encourage vice, saying the forbearance does not suit the obstinate and headstrong, who must be broken as by the strokes of a hammer, and warns against both crushing the weak and flattering the evil.
Clarke reports that a rabbi cites the verse with an extra word, his force, not found in the present Hebrew text, and admits he had put it into his own translation before meeting the remark.
Gill notes that the first verb may mean to grow dim, like a lamp for want of oil, which is why one old version reads instead, he shall shine.
Ellicott says the Greek rendering quoted in the Gospel, in his name shall the Gentiles hope, is a paraphrase rather than a translation.
themes: A calling carried to the end

5.pericope_label: Thus saith God the LORD, he that created the heavens, and stretched them out ... I the LORD have called thee in righteousness, and will hold thine hand, and will keep thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the Gentiles
debates: What called thee in righteousness means: Gill offers three renderings, in a righteous manner, unto righteousness, and with righteousness, while Calvin sets aside the reading that makes it the end of the calling, remarking that the text does not say called to righteousness, and takes the word adverbially as denoting stability.

What a covenant of the people means: Clarke reports manuscripts giving the everlasting covenant instead and argues the noun should be rendered covenant sacrifice; Ellicott limits the people to Israel and makes the servant the covenant itself; Wesley refuses the limitation and reads all people, Jews and Gentiles alike.
outliers: Calvin explains the pile of divine titles by the incredibility of the promise, especially when the outward aspect of things runs directly contrary to it.
Henry reads the titles as marking God the fountain of being in three worlds, and finds a purpose in prefixing them, that redemption was to maintain the honour of the Creator.
Gill sets aside two Jewish readings that make the called person the prophet himself or the people of Israel.
Calvin raises the objection that the covenant was ratified two thousand years before, and answers that it had its foundation in Christ and was ratified only in the seed of Abraham.
themes: A calling both lawful and lasting
The servant given as the covenant

7.pericope_label: To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house. I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images. Behold, the former things are come to pass, and new things do I declare: before they spring forth I tell you of them
debates: What the former things are: Keil and Delitzsch take them as the rise of Cyrus and the agitation of the nations it caused, while Gill makes them the whole chain of fulfilled prediction from Abraham down to the captivity of the ten tribes.

How the second clause of the eighth verse should be read: Gill reports a variant giving a different word for the name and connects it with a divine name still used among the Jews and the Turks, while Calvin knows the same reading and rejects it, denying the word is ever a proper name of God.
outliers: Ellicott remarks that the prophet must have felt the contrast between this commission and his own, which had been to make eyes blind.
Calvin says God is not instructing Christ what to do, as though he needed teaching, but speaking for our sake, that we may know why the Father sent him.

Calvin supplies a test for genuine prediction drawn from plants that bud before they fruit: God does not foretell what has already begun and might be conjectured, but speaks before anything has occurred from which a conjecture could be formed.
Keil and Delitzsch decline in passing to settle whether the captivity was the prophet’s historical or only his ideal standpoint.
themes: A name shared with no one

10.pericope_label: Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise from the end of the earth, ye that go down to the sea, and all that is therein; the isles, and the inhabitants thereof. Let the wilderness and the cities thereof lift up their voice ... Let them give glory unto the LORD, and declare his praise in the islands
debates: How the geography should be read: Ellicott takes Kedar as the one point of localisation and builds a precise eastern map from it, while Calvin treats the places as a part standing for the whole and his annotator argues that sea, islands, deserts and mountains are ingredients of one picture, so that it is absurd to read the ends widely and the middle strictly.

Whether the clause about those who go down to the sea is sound: Clarke suspects a copyist wrote one Hebrew phrase for another and that the line should read, let the sea roar, but declines to put his own conjecture into the translation, and notes the versions do not support a second one.
outliers: Clarke attacks preachers who make the rock Christ and its inhabitants believers, recalling a clergyman who spent an hour on four such heads, and says all of it is true in itself but false of the words it was built on.

Calvin says the new song cannot be sung except by renewed men, since it must proceed from the deepest feeling of the heart, and that to mutter or sing to oneself is impossible for anyone who has tasted the grace of God.
themes: Desert and city called to praise
A song the old world had not heard

13.pericope_label: The LORD shall go forth as a mighty man, he shall stir up jealousy like a man of war: he shall cry, yea, roar; he shall prevail against his enemies. I have long time holden my peace; I have been still, and refrained myself: now will I cry like a travailing woman; I will destroy and devour at once. I will make waste mountains and hills, and dry up all their herbs
debates: Whether the mountains and rivers stand for anything: Gill reads them as kingdoms and governors and Ellicott as the kingdoms of the two great rivers, while Calvin refuses the method outright, saying there is no necessity for such ingenious speculations and the plain meaning is that no army can resist God.

What the last clause of the fourteenth verse says: Ellicott renders it not I will destroy and devour but I pant and gasp, taking the verbs as the cries of the travailing woman rather than destructive acts, against every other reading here.
outliers: Henry declines to settle whether these verses are the song the Gentile world is to sing or a prophecy of what will make way for it, saying it comes all to one.
Clarke reports an extra word behind the old Greek version turning the clause into a question, shall I always keep silence, and thinks it dropped out by a transcriber’s mistake.

Calvin guards the maternal figure twice, granting that such things may be thought inapplicable to God but that his love can be expressed no other way, and noting that the prophet at once adds the lion and the giant so that the majesty is not lowered.
Keil and Delitzsch note a fresh example of the prophet’s habit of returning at the close of a period to the word it began with.
themes: Love figured as a mother in labour

16.pericope_label: And I will bring the blind by a way that they knew not; I will lead them in paths that they have not known: I will make darkness light before them, and crooked things straight. These things will I do unto them, and not forsake them. They shall be turned back, they shall be greatly ashamed, that trust in graven images
debates: Who the blind are: Wesley makes them the Gentiles, Gill reports a Jewish reading applying the verse to Israel, and Keil and Delitzsch define them by condition rather than nation, as those deprived of sight by their own sin.

How literally the shame of the idolaters is meant: Ellicott reads it historically of the victories of Cyrus over the idols he was to overthrow, while Keil and Delitzsch keep it general and make the fall of the false religions the redemption of the heathen.
Which way the turning back goes: Gill allows both conversion from idols to the living God and the flight of those not converted, seeking rocks and mountains to hide them.
outliers: Calvin argues it is often good for us to have no way open and even to be blinded, since so long as a plank is left that we think we can seize we turn to it with our whole heart, and that it is better to be blind men guided by God than to build labyrinths by our own sagacity.

Clarke works through the grammar of the last clause, noting the written form is a second person, that forty manuscripts carry the letter that would settle it, and that the pronoun does duty for a phrase with a preposition.

Clarke says the same grammatical point, applied to a famous passage, has cleared up a difficulty that puzzled expositors for two thousand years and set the learned quarrelling over whether Jephthah sacrificed his daughter.
Calvin answers the objection that no one would say to an image, thou art my god, by arguing that men ascribe God’s power to images while confessing he is in heaven.
themes: A road unknown to those on it
Trust in images put to shame

18.pericope_label: Hear, ye deaf; and look, ye blind, that ye may see. Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger that I sent? who is blind as he that is perfect, and blind as the LORD’s servant? Seeing many things, but thou observest not; opening the ears, but he heareth not
debates: Who is addressed in the eighteenth verse: Gill reports a Jewish reading that takes it of Israel and prefers to read it of the impenitent Gentiles, while Calvin says that although the reproach falls directly on the Jews he would rather have it condemn all men.

What the word rendered perfect means: Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both refuse the received sense, the one giving the devoted or surrendered one and noting its kinship with the modern words for a Muslim and for Islam, the other rejecting a proposal that makes it the purchased one and settling on the confidant of God.

Whether the nineteenth verse is the prophets’ reproach or their accusers’: Calvin reports an interpretation making it the retort of wicked men against the prophets and rejects it, since the following verse explains the blindness in terms that cannot apply to prophets.
outliers: Henry answers the objection that God commands what we cannot do, comparing the man with the withered hand, who could not stretch it out but would not have been healed had he not attempted it.
Calvin observes that blind and deaf are not used here as a few verses earlier, where they described men overwhelmed by affliction rather than men shutting their eyes in the light.

Clarke proposes reading deaf for blind in the last clause, calling the mistake palpable and the correction admissible even had there been no authority for it, and remarks that the Masoretes perceived a fault in the next verse without knowing where it lay.
Ellicott refuses outright the transfer of the twentieth verse to the sufferings of Christ, calling it scarcely tenable.
themes: A command given to those who cannot obey

21.pericope_label: The LORD is well pleased for his righteousness’ sake; he will magnify the law, and make it honourable. But this is a people robbed and spoiled ... Who gave Jacob for a spoil, and Israel to the robbers? did not the LORD, he against whom we have sinned? Therefore he hath poured upon him the fury of his anger, and the strength of battle
debates: How the twenty-first verse should be read: Calvin reports two other renderings, that the Lord hath so willed it and that he is merciful, before settling on the Lord is willing, while Ellicott changes the tenses to give, the Lord was well pleased and made his law great.

Which captivity the closing verses describe: Ellicott says it is hard to tell whether the exiles in Babylon are meant or a second and later exile, and inclines on balance to the second, while Gill refers the whole without hesitation to the Roman siege.
outliers: Clarke notes that where the received text has law the old Greek version read praise, and that two old versions read they have sinned where the Hebrew has we have sinned.

Calvin says everybody acknowledges God to be the author of all things, but that men will be ashamed to confess adverse events his chastisements, there being nothing they are persuaded of with more difficulty.
Calvin draws from the question of the twenty-third verse the use of all threatening, that God does not punish as though he delighted in vengeance but that we may be on our guard for the time to come.
Wesley explains the forbearance by saying God will not be forward to destroy those who profess the true religion, lest his law be exposed to contempt on that occasion.
themes: A law made great and honourable
